page.title: Solar Inverter for Off Grid: Size It Per 120 V Leg, Not by Total Watts
page.h1: The best solar inverter for off grid, and what each 120 V leg can actually carry
page.desc: 48 V off-grid inverters compared by what their 120 V circuits really get: EG4 6000XP, Sun Gold Power SPH6548P, Growatt SPE/SPF and Victron MultiPlus-II, with today's prices.
page.answer: Short answer. The best solar inverter for off grid in a US home is a 48V all-in-one with built-in MPPT and 120/240V split phase output: the EG4 6000XP. Size it per leg, not by total: its 6,000W is 3,000W max on each 120V leg. The Growatt SPF 5000US puts out 240V only.

page.after:
What the differences mean

  • Per-leg capacity. EG4 6000XP: 6,000 W ÷ 2 legs = 3,000 W per 120 V leg. An 1,800 W microwave plus a 1,500 W space heater on the same leg is 1,800 + 1,500 = 3,300 W. That overloads the leg even though it is only 3,300 ÷ 6,000 = 55% of the nameplate.
  • Cost per kW today. SPH6548P: $1,035 ÷ 6.5 kW = $159. EG4 6000XP: $1,499.99 ÷ 6 kW = $250. Growatt SPE 6000 US: $1,599 ÷ 6 kW = $267. The SPH6548P is $464.99 cheaper than the 6000XP for 500 W more rated output.
  • Idle drain on the battery. EG4 6000XP: about 50 W on battery × 24 h = 1.2 kWh a day, or 1.2 ÷ 5.12 = 23% of one 5.12 kWh 48 V server-rack battery such as the {buy:sungoldpower-sg48100p-48v-100ah}. Victron 48/5000/70-95: 19 W × 24 h = 0.46 kWh a day.
  • Solar string headroom. SPH6548P: 550 V ÷ 480 V = 1.15, so its PV inputs accept 15% more open-circuit string voltage than the 6000XP's. That headroom matters on cold mornings, when panel voltage rises.
  • Surge, rated vs measured. EG4 rates the 6000XP at 12,000 W for about 3.5 s. The Solar Lab measured 7.3–7.5 kW for 3–5 s, and 7.5 ÷ 12 = 63% of the rating.

Size an off-grid inverter per 120 V leg, not by total watts

A US split-phase panel has two 120 V legs (L1 and L2) that together make 240 V. A 240 V load such as a well pump draws from both legs at once. Every 120 V circuit (fridge, microwave, kettle, space heater) sits on only one leg. EG4's manual lists the 6000XP's maximum continuous line wattage as 3,000 W against 6,000 W nominal. Jonathan Richter at SolarTech Online states that the unit cannot balance loads between legs: 'If you have 4000W of appliances on one 120V leg, the inverter will overload.' EG4 describes the 6000XP as a transformerless, high-frequency design. So for a mostly 120 V home, plan breakers so that neither leg's simultaneous load goes over 3,000 W, or add a second unit. The manual also notes that the internal neutral-ground bond is off by default (setting 26). An off-grid system with no utility service needs exactly one bond, either at the inverter or at the panel, not both.

Sun Gold Power's SPH6548P listing gives the 6,500 W total, a 13,000 VA peak and a choice of split-phase or 120 V single-phase output, without a per-leg wattage. If most of your load is 120 V, ask Sun Gold Power for the L1/L2 rating before you lay out the panel. Victron's 120 V MultiPlus-II puts out a single 120 V leg per unit. Two units joined over VE.Bus give 120/240 V. In the 120 V line, the 48/3000/35-50 carries UL 1741, and the 48/5000/70-95 carries UL 1741 and UL 458. The similarly named 48/5000/70-50 belongs to Victron's 230 V line: 230 VAC at 50 Hz, with EN/IEC rather than UL listings. It does not suit a US panel.

Not recommended

Growatt SPF 5000US as a drop-in for a US home or cabin. It looks cheap at $750, but Signature Solar's listing states 'This Unit is 240V output only', and Growatt's own US page tags it 230 Vac. Ordinary 120 V outlets need Growatt's separate ATS 5000T-ES split-phase transformer, and the unit carries a 2-year warranty against 5 years for the EG4 6000XP. If you only need 240 V (a well pump or shop motor), it works. For a normal 120/240 V panel, a split-phase all-in-one costs less once the transformer is added.
